transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is, mostly at night, once I start eating, it’s like I’m watching myself do it. I’ll be thinking, “Stop, that’s enough,” but then my hands just keep going back for more anyway.

It sounds silly saying it out loud. I used to be a pretty controlled person at work—plans, schedules, drawings, all that—and now I can’t seem to manage something as basic as stopping when I’m eating.
Do you feel like you're unable to control your eating once you start?

Yes… that’s pretty much it. Especially at night. I’ll start eating and there’s this part of me that’s watching it happen, like, “Alright, stop now, that’s enough,” but then I just keep reaching for more anyway.

It’s strange because I can be very particular about other things—at work I used to catch tiny measurement mistakes in plans, you know, things other people would miss—but with this, once it starts, I don’t feel like I’m the one steering it anymore.
Do you feel like you're losing control over other things besides eating?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean… eating is the one that stands out. Other things, I still feel like I can keep a handle on, more or less.

Though, you know, since retiring from managing projects—or, well, stepping back from that kind of work—I do notice my days can get a bit loose. I used to have drawings to review, deadlines, people coming into my office with problems… and now if the day gets away from me, it’s not quite the same thing as losing control, I don’t think.

So… I haven’t really noticed it in the same way outside of eating.
Do you feel guilty or ashamed after these episodes of eating?

I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I don’t sit there naming it “guilt” exactly.

Sometimes afterward I do sort of think, “Well, that was stupid,” or I try not to think about it at all. But then my mind goes off to something else, like whether I forgot to lock the garage or if I left a light on—little things like that. I used to be very methodical about checking things, especially on job sites, so it’s funny what sticks with you.

So… ashamed? I’m not sure. Uncomfortable with myself, maybe, but I don’t know if I’d use those exact words.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over time?

I don’t really keep track closely, to be honest. I mean, I know how my clothes fit, and sometimes I’ll think a shirt feels tighter or looser, but I’m not someone who’s writing the numbers down or anything.

Back when I was working, I paid attention to numbers all day—dimensions, budgets, schedules—and funny enough, with my own weight I sort of avoid looking too carefully. So… significant changes? I’m not sure I could say. Nothing I’ve really measured in a clear way.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset right before these episodes of eating happen?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear pattern like that. Sometimes I might be a bit wound up beforehand, but then again, I can get wound up about ordinary things too—mail piling up, a bill sitting on the counter, whether I was supposed to call someone back.

It’s not like I sit there and think, “I’m upset, so now this is going to happen.” It’s more… the eating happens, and afterward I try to piece together what was going on before it. But I’m not sure. I suppose I haven’t paid attention to the “right before” part very well.
Do you find yourself doing other things compulsively, like checking things over and over?

I mean… checking things, yes, but I don’t know if I’d call it compulsive exactly. I’ve always been someone who goes back over things, especially when I was working—plans, measurements, whether something was signed off properly. In that line of work, if you miss one little thing, it can become a whole problem later.

At home, I might double-check a door or look again to see if I turned something off, but I don’t know that it’s “over and over.” Sometimes I just don’t trust my memory. I’ll be halfway into the next room and think, “Did I actually do that, or did I just think about doing it?” That happens more than I’d like, but I’m not sure where the line is between being careful and… whatever you’d call it.
Do you feel an overwhelming urge to eat when you start, or is it more that you just can't seem to stop once you've begun?

It’s more the second one, I think. Once I start, especially at night, it’s like… I’m watching myself do it. Part of me is saying, “Alright, that’s enough, stop now,” but then my hand is already going back for something else.

It sounds strange saying it out loud. I used to have to be very deliberate with things at work—drawings, schedules, approvals, all that—and I’m not used to feeling like I can’t get myself to follow the instruction I’m giving myself. But that’s what it feels like. Not so much some big dramatic urge at the very start, more like once it’s going, I can’t seem to put the brakes on.
Do you feel like you lose control over other activities besides eating?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, with other things… I can get caught up in something, like looking for a paper I misplaced or going back through a list, and then suddenly I’ve spent more time on it than I meant to. But that feels different somehow.

When I was working, there were always a hundred little details, and if you didn’t chase one down it could come back to bite you later. So I got used to following a thread maybe longer than other people would. Even now, I’ll start straightening a drawer or trying to remember where I put something, and then—well, my wife used to say I could turn a simple thing into a whole project.

But “lose control” sounds a bit strong. Besides the eating, I don’t know that I’ve noticed anything else where I feel that same… inability to stop. Not clearly, anyway.
Do you feel like you lose control when engaging in other activities, not just eating?

I don’t really know. I mean, I can get wrapped up in things, sure. If I’m sorting something or trying to fix some little problem, I might keep at it longer than I meant to. I’ve always been that way a bit—when I was managing jobs, you couldn’t just leave a loose end sitting there, because it would show up later and cost you twice the trouble.

But that’s not quite the same as what happens with eating. With other things, I usually feel like I could stop if I had to, or if someone interrupted me. I might be annoyed, but I’d stop. So… no, I haven’t really noticed that same loss of control with other activities. Not in the same way.
Do you ever feel like you're unable to stop an activity other than eating once you've started it?

I don’t think so. Not in the way you mean, anyway.

I can be stubborn with things, like if I start looking through a box of old papers, suddenly I’m separating receipts from manuals and then wondering why I kept a warranty for something we got rid of ten years ago. That can go on longer than I intended. My wife used to tease me about that—said I’d make a filing system for a junk drawer if nobody stopped me.

But if I had to stop, I think I could. It doesn’t feel like the eating does. It’s more like I get sidetracked or overly focused, not that I’m unable to stop.
Do you feel guilty after these episodes of eating?

I don’t know… guilty is a hard word. Sometimes afterward I feel foolish, I guess, like, “Why did I do that?” But then I start thinking about whether I had a proper meal earlier, or if I was just tired, or if I’d been pacing around the kitchen too long.

My wife used to say I could turn anything into an investigation, and maybe I do that with this too—try to explain it instead of just sitting with it. So… maybe there’s some guilt in there, but I’m not always sure that’s what I’d call it.
Do you feel distressed after these episodes of eating?

Distressed… I’m not sure. I mean, I don’t usually sit there and think, “I’m distressed,” if that makes sense. It’s more muddled than that.

Sometimes I feel unsettled afterward, like I want to clean up or get things back in order. I’ll start wiping the counter or putting things away, and then I’m thinking about whether the pantry needs reorganizing—my wife used to say I could avoid any feeling if there was a shelf to straighten.

So, I don’t know. Maybe there’s discomfort after, yes, but I’m not sure I’d call it distress exactly. It’s hard for me to pin down.
Do you feel upset or unhappy after these episodes of eating?

Upset or unhappy… I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly every time. Sometimes I’m just annoyed with myself, like when you misplace a tool you know you just had in your hand, and then you spend twenty minutes looking for it even though it’s right there on the bench.

After eating like that, I can get quiet, maybe a little down, but then I’ll start thinking about practical things—what needs washing, whether I should take the trash out, whether I should’ve bought something different at the store. I tend to drift into that kind of thinking.

So… maybe sometimes unhappy, yes, but I don’t always recognize it that way in the moment.
Do you think your eating episodes are triggered by feeling emotional?

Emotional… I’m not sure. I haven’t really tracked it that way. I mean, sometimes I’m tired or irritated, but whether that’s what starts it, I don’t know.

I tend to notice more concrete things, like what time it is or what’s in the kitchen. Funny, at work I used to be good at finding patterns in schedules and drawings, but with myself it’s messier. I can look at a building plan and tell you where the problem is, but with this… I’m not sure I can say it’s because I’m feeling emotional.
Do you think your eating episodes happen when you are feeling emotional?

I don’t really know. I mean, it might, but I haven’t caught it in the act, if that makes sense.

Sometimes I’ll realize afterward that I was wound up about something, but other times it just seems like I was in the kitchen and one thing led to another. Like if I’m looking for something in a drawer, I’ll end up sorting the whole drawer and forget why I opened it. It’s kind of like that—hard to say what started it.

So… emotional, maybe sometimes, but I can’t say I’ve noticed a clear pattern.
Do you think your eating episodes are usually triggered by feeling stressed, anxious, or upset?

I don’t know that I can say “usually.” Stress and anxious and upset all sound very specific, like you’d be able to put a little flag on it and say, “That’s the reason,” and I’m not sure I can.

Sometimes I’ve had a rough day, sure, but sometimes it’s more like I’m just standing there in the kitchen and then I’m eating. Like when you go into the garage to get one screwdriver and end up rearranging a shelf because you noticed the screws were mixed up. It doesn’t always feel like there was some big feeling before it.

So… maybe sometimes, but I haven’t noticed it clearly enough to say it’s usually from stress or being upset.
Do you think your eating episodes are usually triggered by feeling emotional?

I know you’re asking “usually,” and that’s the part I get stuck on. I haven’t really been able to pin it to being emotional most of the time.

Sometimes I think back and wonder if I was bothered about something, but in the moment it doesn’t feel that clear. It’s more like… I’m in the kitchen, I notice something, then another thing, and suddenly it’s happened. Like at work, when one small issue in a plan turns into checking the whole set of drawings—except this isn’t useful like that.

So I guess I’d say I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed a reliable emotional trigger.
Do you think your eating episodes happen when you're feeling emotional?

I’m still not totally sure. I know that’s probably not the most helpful answer, but I haven’t caught a clean connection like, “Oh, I’m sad, so now this happens.”

Sometimes afterward I might think, well, maybe I was irritated or wound up, but during it I’m not really labeling it that way. It’s more like one thing rolls into another. Like when I’m reviewing a project and I mean to check one measurement, then suddenly I’m three pages deep looking at something else entirely.

So… it could be emotional sometimes, but I can’t honestly say I’ve noticed that clearly.
Do you think your eating episodes are usually triggered by feeling emotional?

I know we’re back on “usually,” and I don’t mean to be difficult, but I just don’t have a solid answer for that.

I can think of times when maybe I was bothered, but it’s not like I’ve kept notes or anything. I used to keep pretty detailed notes on jobs—materials, schedule changes, little mistakes that would come back to bite you later—and if I had something like that for this, maybe I could tell you. But just going from memory, it’s muddy.

So… no, I can’t really say it’s usually triggered by feeling emotional. I haven’t noticed a clear pattern.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether binge episodes are usually triggered by feeling emotional, but the provided symptom profile does not include an item about emotional triggers.

patient.answer:
I know we’re back on “usually,” and I don’t mean to be difficult, but I just don’t have a solid answer for that.

I can think of times when maybe I was bothered, but it’s not like I’ve kept notes or anything. I used to keep pretty detailed notes on jobs—materials, schedule changes, little mistakes that would come back to bite you later—and if I had something like that for this, maybe I could tell you. But just going from memory, it’s muddy.

So… no, I can’t really say it’s usually triggered by feeling emotional. I haven’t noticed a clear pattern.
